exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with tremor, sweating, and agitation after stopping heroin; what is the most appropriate immediate management — use a partial opioid agonist (buprenorphine) to control withdrawal while avoiding full agonists that may precipitate relapse.

A patient with severe alcohol dependence develops seizures; which lab test helps gauge severity and guide treatment — check serum gamma‑glutamyl transferase (GGT) and carbohydrate‑deficient transferrin; high levels indicate chronic heavy use and risk of delirium tremens.

During a ward round you notice a patient on long‑term benzodiazepines also drinks locally brewed alcohol; what red flag should prompt urgent review — additive CNS depression risking respiratory failure; consider tapering benzodiazepine and offering detox.

In a rural clinic, urine drug screen is unavailable; how can you still assess opioid dependence severity — use the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) to quantify withdrawal signs and guide treatment.

A pregnant woman with opioid use disorder seeks help; which medication is safest for maintenance therapy — buprenorphine (or buprenorphine‑naloxone avoided) because it has lower fetal risk than methadone.
You suspect injection‑drug‑related endocarditis; what bedside clue supports this diagnosis — presence of new murmur plus track marks and fever, prompting urgent echocardiography.

A patient with HIV and alcohol use disorder is started on antiretroviral therapy; which drug interaction must you monitor — avoid protease inhibitors with high‑dose alcohol due to increased hepatotoxicity.
Family therapy is recommended in the Kenyan protocol; what is its main benefit for SUD patients — improves communication, reduces relapse rates, and strengthens support networks.
ai.title: Substance Use Disorder
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: A chronic brain disorder marked by compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences. Diagnosis relies on DSM‑5 criteria; severity is graded by the number of criteria met. Management combines psychosocial therapy and pharmacotherapy, adapted to low‑resource settings.

b: 2–3 criteria: mild SUD
4–5 criteria: moderate SUD
6 or more criteria: severe SUD
sections.p: Substance Use Disorder (SUD) is defined by DSM‑5 as a problematic pattern of substance use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, manifested by at least two of eleven criteria within a 12‑month period.

b: Mild: early intervention, brief counseling
Moderate: structured therapy, possible pharmacotherapy
Severe: intensive rehab, medication‑assisted treatment
sections.p: Severity is staged by the number of criteria met (mild, moderate, severe). Clinicians also consider physiological dependence (withdrawal, tolerance) and psychosocial impact.

b: Co‑occurring HIV infection (self‑medication, stigma)
Chronic pain from untreated injuries or TB spine
Unemployment, poverty, and limited recreational options
Use of locally brewed alcohol, khat, or herbal stimulants
sections.p: Risk factors are multifactorial, with psychosocial, genetic, and environmental contributors. In East African low‑resource hospitals, common precipitating conditions include:

b: Repeated requests for the same drug
Neglected personal hygiene, weight loss
Legal or financial problems
Physical signs: track marks, tremor, conjunctival injection
sections.p: Patients may present with withdrawal syndromes, intoxication, or complications of chronic use. Typical clues:
Testing confirms substance exposure, screens for comorbidities, and guides safe medication choices.

t.b: Identifies recent use of opioids, benzodiazepines, cannabis, amphetamines; a positive result supports diagnosis and informs withdrawal planning.
Detects hepatic injury from alcohol or hepatotoxic drugs; elevated ALT/AST >2× ULN suggests need for cautious medication selection.
Screens for HIV, a common comorbidity; a positive result mandates integrated care and influences choice of opioid agonist therapy.
Looks for anemia or leukopenia that may indicate chronic infection (e.g., TB) or nutritional deficiency; guides overall management.

t.a: If laboratory unavailable: clinical withdrawal scales (e.g., CIWA‑Ar for alcohol, COWS for opioids)
t.b: Quantifies severity of withdrawal; guides need for pharmacologic support when labs are not accessible.

b: Severe alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens, seizures)
Opioid overdose (respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils)
Benzodiazepine + alcohol co‑intoxication (marked CNS depression)
Infective endocarditis from injection drug use
Acute pancreatitis from heavy alcohol use
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.

b: Stabilize airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if hypoxic.
Withdrawal: benzodiazepines for alcohol, buprenorphine‑naloxone for opioids, clonidine for mild opioid withdrawal when buprenorphine unavailable.
Avoid benzodiazepines in patients with severe respiratory disease or concurrent alcohol intoxication due to additive depression.
Psychosocial: motivational interviewing, cognitive‑behavioral therapy, and family therapy (shown to improve retention in Kenyan protocols).
Relapse prevention: link to community support groups, address housing or employment needs.
sections.p: A stepped approach: stabilize, treat withdrawal, initiate long‑term therapy, and address psychosocial factors.

b: Regular outpatient visits to monitor abstinence and mental health.
Screen for HIV, hepatitis B/C, TB; vaccinate where appropriate.
Provide brief interventions for hazardous drinking in primary care.
Educate patients on safe use of prescribed medications.
sections.p: Long‑term success depends on continuity of care and addressing comorbidities.

b: Acute psychosis from schizophrenia – differentiate by presence of delusions without substance trigger.
Medication side‑effects (e.g., anticholinergic toxicity) – look for specific drug exposure history.
Somatic symptom disorder – focus on excessive health worries rather than compulsive drug use.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic SUD or share overlapping features.

b: False‑negative urine screens for newer synthetic cannabinoids; rely on history.
Elevated liver enzymes may be from malaria or hepatitis, not only alcohol.
Normal vital signs during early opioid overdose; watch for delayed respiratory depression.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe withdrawal with seizures or delirium tremens
Respiratory rate < 8/min or oxygen saturation < 90% after opioid use
Unconsciousness or inability to protect airway
